Plain Functions, Not Classes

Why controllers and services here are grouped functions, not a Laravel-style class hierarchy.

Every Laravel controller you've written extends a base Controller class; every model extends Eloquent. Inheritance is baked in from the first line. Express itself has no equivalent expectation — a "controller" is just whatever function you hand a route — and this project doesn't invent one to fill the gap. Controllers and services here are plain functions, grouped per module, not classes:

// Figure 0.2: two of ticket.controller.js's exported functions (excerpt)
export const getTicketById = asyncHandler(async (req, res) => {
  const ticket = await ticketService.getTicketById(req.params.id, req.user);

  if (!ticket) {
    throw new ApiError(404, `Ticket ${req.params.id} not found`);
  }

  sendResource(res, ticket);
});

export const createTicket = asyncHandler(async (req, res) => {
  const ticket = await ticketService.createTicket({ ...req.body, customerId: req.user.id });
  sendResource(res, ticket, 201);
});

ticket.controller.js is a file full of functions like these, not a class with methods. ticket.service.js, imported at the top as ticketService, is the same shape one layer down.

Where does dependency injection go, then — how does a controller get "its" service without a constructor to inject one into? It doesn't need to: an imported module is already a singleton in Node. import * as ticketService from '../services/ticket.service.js' gives every file that imports it the exact same object, created once, the first time anything imports it. A DI container exists to solve the problem of wiring up and sharing single instances of things — Node's module system already does that for free, so there's nothing left for a container to add.

The same reasoning rules out a Resource/Transformer class hierarchy for shaping responses, too — covered properly once there's a response to shape. For now, the pattern to notice: this codebase reaches for plain functions and plain objects first, and only reaches for more structure (a class, a container, a framework convention) when plain functions stop being enough — never as the default starting point.
